title: Shraddha Kapoor Dances Through Labour Pain. The 'Eetha' Teaser Is the Transformation Nobody Saw Coming.
excerpt: Maddock smuggled the teaser into theatres with 'Cocktail 2,' it leaked, it went viral, and suddenly Shraddha was beating the actual released film on Google Trends. This is her swing for the fences.
body:
It was supposed to be the warm-up act. The teaser for **Eetha** played in cinemas tagged onto **Maddock Films'** *Cocktail 2* — a supporting trailer before the main event. Within hours of audiences spotting it, someone filmed the screen, the clip leaked online, and **Shraddha Kapoor** went from a search-interest score of 4 to a flat 100. She wasn't even in the film people had paid to see. She still walked out with the day.

That is the kind of entrance most actors spend a career chasing.

**A folk legend, reborn**

https://x.com/SumitkadeI/status/2069352831031873790

*Eetha* is the biopic of **Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar**, the legendary Maharashtrian Tamasha performer who turned Lavani into something close to scripture for rural folk theatre. Vithabai's life was the stuff of myth — she reportedly delivered a child backstage and returned to the stage to finish her performance, refusing to let the show stop. The teaser leans straight into that legend: in its most arresting beat, Shraddha's Eetha dances *through* labour, and the internet has not recovered.

Directed by **Laxman Utekar** and backed by **Dinesh Vijan's** Maddock Films, the film hits theatres on August 28, 2026, in the thick of the Raksha Bandhan corridor. Running two minutes and eighteen seconds, the teaser is rich with atmosphere — vibrant Lavani costumes, elaborate sets, the heat and noise of a Tamasha crowd calling for their dancer. Then Shraddha appears, and the conventional star-entry setup quietly dissolves into something rawer.

**The boldest she's ever looked**

Let's be honest about what this is. Shraddha Kapoor has spent years as Bollywood's reliable girl-next-door — *Aashiqui 2*, *Stree*, the *Thumkeshwari* cameo that, fans will remind you, snatched a fair bit of *Cocktail 2*'s thunder. *Eetha* is a different animal entirely. The transformation here goes well past costume; it's in the body language, the expressions, the way she holds a stage that isn't a music video set. This is the kind of role that gets called "career-defining" before a single ticket is sold — and for once the hype might be earned.

> "Omg!! Phenomenal! Trust me, I'm not exaggerating but I literally got teary eyed watching her performance. This is going to be epic." — a fan reaction that captured the mood online

The comparisons came fast and pointed, the loudest of them aimed at *Gangubai Kathiawadi*. "Shraddha legit owned every frame with her grace and magnificence," one viewer wrote, framing *Eetha* as a direct challenge to Alia Bhatt's most decorated performance. Whether or not that's fair, it tells you the bar audiences are setting. With music by **Ajay–Atul** — the composers who understand Maharashtra's sound better than almost anyone working — and Utekar's eye for rooted, unglamorous detail, *Eetha* is being talked about as a genuine awards contender.

**A Raksha Bandhan pile-up**

August 28 won't be a clear runway. *Eetha* is set to clash with **Sidharth Malhotra's** supernatural drama *Vvan*, and it sits two days behind Yash's mammoth *Toxic* (August 26) in the same festive stretch — a four-film logjam that also includes *Khosla Ka Ghosla 2*. A grounded, female-led biopic squaring up against pan-India spectacle and a horror tentpole is a real test. But word-of-mouth films have a way of finding daylight in a crowded weekend, and one forum regular's prediction has been making the rounds: "Easy 200 crores, even if the film is very average. Public is very excited."

For diaspora audiences, a Marathi-rooted story like this usually travels through Maddock's standard playbook — a theatrical run across PVR INOX's international screens and Indian-cinema slates in the US, UK and Canada, followed by a streaming home (the studio leans Netflix and Prime Video) within a couple of months. Subtitles will matter here; the Lavani and the language are the whole point, and a good translation will decide how much of Vithabai's fire survives the journey.

Shraddha said little in the teaser. She didn't need to. She danced, the crowd roared, and a folk legend who once refused to let the show stop got the comeback vehicle she deserved — carried by an actor finally daring to be more than likeable.
